David Ricardo had a change of heart. In 1819, testifying before Parliament, Ricardo — whose </span><em>Principles of Political Economy</em><span> has a better claim than Adam Smith’s </span><em>The Wealth of Nations</em><span> to be considered the founding document of the field we call economics — had dismissed concerns that the Industrial Revolution then in progress would hurt workers. But by 1821, when he published the third edition of his book, he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c3647b51-3042-4ebb-9f04-4e336a93cc41?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">admitted</a><span> that his views “had undergone a considerable change.” He went on to declare that</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(33, 37, 41)" style="color: rgb(33, 37, 41);">the substitution of machinery for human labour, is often very injurious to the interests of the class of labourers</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(33, 37, 41)" style="color: rgb(33, 37, 41);">and that</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span data-color="rgb(33, 37, 41)" style="color: rgb(33, 37, 41);">the opinion entertained by the labouring class, that the employment of machinery is frequently detrimental to their interests, is not founded on prejudice and error, but is conformable to the correct principles of political economy.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the language of modern economics, Ricardo had come to the conclusion that the Industrial Revolution was bringing about “capital-biased technological change”: change that, other things equal, reduced the demand for labor while increasing the demand for capital. And as he realized, strong capital-biased technology can drive wages down even as it raises GDP.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let me note, by the way, that Ricardo was willing both to change his views in the face of new evidence and to admit that he had been wrong in the past. That kind of intellectual maturity and honesty is hard to find these days.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Was Ricardo right to conclude, after reconsidering, that the introduction of machinery was hurting workers? Economists are still debating that question, in part because economic data on early 19</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span>-century Britain are limited. But Ricardo’s reversal shows that one of the biggest debates surrounding AI — will it hurt workers? — has a very long history.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI itself, by contrast, has a very short history, and what we think we know about its economics is changing rapidly. My own views have evolved since the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eddd2988-51ae-41a9-9629-bd7aff647d79?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">last time I wrote about this subject</a><span> less than 4 months ago — hey, if Ricardo’s views could change, so can mine.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Today, then, I will offer another entry in my series of primers on issues related to AI, this one revisiting the question of how this powerful but confusing technology may affect incomes and the distribution of income going forward. Where Ricardo became more pessimistic about the potential impact of technology on the relationship between capital and labor, I am somewhat less pessimistic than I was a few months ago — or at least more skeptical about some of the extreme scenarios. I am, however, increasingly concerned about how AI will affect the reward or lack thereof for many traditionally valuable skills.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: I’m hardly alone in saying this — </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/131c6a05-fc4e-49b1-898c-e2338b7f6ba0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Wirecutter</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fe02a633-97e9-41c3-b553-5f2d73414230?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Eater.com</a><span>, and plenty of others have noted the same drawbacks. But anyway, let’s go through the many reasons why pizza cutters are not fit for the job they’re named after.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First, it’s hard to make a very strong cut with a pizza cutter. This is because when you roll a cutting wheel forward, your hand isn’t pushing straight down — it’s pushing forward and down at the same time, meaning that only some of the force from your cut is being delivered to the pizza itself. That makes your job harder. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of that, the amount of force that goes into the pizza isn’t constant across the cut. As you extend your arm across the pizza while pushing the roller forward, the angle changes — when the cutter is right under your arm, most of the force goes down into the pizza, but when it’s at the far end of the pizza, most of the force is going </span><em>forward</em><span> instead of down. This means that you basically have to do one of three things:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Be very good at dynamically adjusting your force level as you cut</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Roll the pizza wheel back and forth over the pizza several times</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Push down really, really hard the whole time</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The first of these is hard and takes a lot of skill. The second results in little slivers in your pizza — since it’s very hard to keep the wheel in the groove as you cut back and forth — and often causes the dreaded “cheese drag”, in which the wheel drags the cheese right off of the top of the pizza. The third method blunts the cutting wheel, and cuts deep grooves into your cutting board. And all three methods require you to expend a lot of energy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pizza wheels are also notoriously hard to maintain and store. Cleaning cheese off of an exposed, rotating blade is difficult, because the blade keeps spinning as you try to wipe it, and because you’re constantly in danger of slicing yourself on the edge. Storing an exposed blade makes it easier to cut yourself when you reach into the drawer. And </span><em>sharpening </em><span>a circular, rotating blade is extremely difficult. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Fortunately, there are better tools out there for cutting pizza. The first, which works great for thin-crust pizza, is a scissors — either </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/86a8951c-6253-4b5c-b4e8-73133bb05637?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a standard pair of kitchen shears</a><span>, or </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fae463c1-8be2-4c4a-a0ab-992c75961ea0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a dedicated pair of pizza shears</a><span>. Please try pizza shears or rocking pizza cutters, and please try washlets. You’ll thank me. But as you probably guessed, this is really a post about AI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I recently had the pleasure of going to a party in Washington D.C. with a number of lawyers, art history professors, and other educated progressive professionals. This provided me with a great opportunity to get out of my west coast tech-and-econ bubble, and talk to intelligent Americans from other regions and other walks of life.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many of these conversations turned to the topic of artificial intelligence. Not one person that I talked to was positive about the technology. The first man I talked to asked me how “the AI bubble” was going. When I told him that Anthropic was experiencing the fastest revenue growth of any large company in history, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cc89d1b4-9b5b-4cfc-a21a-5a2bfc087a64?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">expects to turn an operating profit</a><span> next quarter, he was astonished.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be fair, not everyone pays close attention to quarterly Anthropic numbers; as recently as late 2025 data center investment was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45790895-1171-4337-b4d0-9211ee82a293?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">still racing ahead of revenue</a><span> and even Dario Amodei</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/377d5ead-7bc4-4628-bc8c-4df8d04b63b9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> didn’t know</a><span> whether his company would go bankrupt. But while observers close to the industry — and econ writers like Yours Truly — simply raised the possibility of a bubble, lots of people seemed to have </span><em>assumed </em><span>that a bubble was definitely in progress, and then not bothered to check up on it later. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other folks I talked to were generally dismissive of the potential of AI, and all were concerned about negative effects. One lawyer told me that he knew some people who used it a little bit, but never used it himself. Another said that it was “about as good as a 2nd-year associate”, but worried that people’s reliance on it would erode their own cognitive abilities. Various other people asserted that AI was flooding their professions with low-quality work.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The art historian was even more negative about AI. She argued that AI couldn’t produce real art, because it lacked human input. When I pointed out the difference between skillfully prompted AI videos and sloppily prompted ones, she did consider it, but it was the first time she had thought about it. She then argued that AI art would deceive people by presenting a distorted version of reality as if it was real. When I pointed out that people had made a similar objection to photography and film, before those were eventually recognized as legitimate and respected art forms, she considered this, but insisted that AI was somehow different.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What’s interesting is that this anecdote doesn’t cleanly fit the polls. 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instead, the left has, for a mix of reasons good and bad, convinced itself that AI is at the same time something to when responding on X in December to a discussion of the possibilities of advanced AI. “Large language models do not, cannot, and will not ‘understand’ anything at all,” </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d1b92aa7-b31d-46d1-90b8-9c6e29e66779?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This idea, that large-language models merely produce statistically plausible word sequences based on training data, without having any idea about what the words refer to, has become the baseline across much of the left-intellectual landscape. Thanks to it, fundamental questions about AI’s capabilities, now and in the future, are considered settled.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This dismissiveness reminds me of the cases of the pizza wheel and the washlet. There is no law of the Universe that useful technologies are adopted quickly by everyone who could make use of them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Historically, countries that adopted gunpowder, industrial technology, computers, and other cutting-edge innovations had an edge over those that turned up their noses at them. Sometimes the consequence was a slightly lower GDP; sometimes the consequence was conquest and colonization. In most cases, economic historians believe that a fear of disrupting existing patterns of power and elite status was behind the decision to eschew new technology. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I worry about the same thing that Dan Kagan-Kans worries about. America as a whole is adopting AI rapidly. But if our educated progressive classes — our lawyers, academics, artists, and so on — turn up their noses, it could damage both their own cultural/political tribe and the country as a whole. In fact, by dismissing AI’s potential — by thinking that the most important technological revolution of the modern age can be waved away as a “bubble” or “fancy autocomplete” or IP theft or slop or whatever — they make it harder to think about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0dc46c32-f237-4c57-ac07-def4297e64d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the actual serious risks AI might pose</a><span>.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">³</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The coming of AI will definitely disrupt many of the relations of status and power in America. As </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73ca0206-5edd-45c5-88ce-ea9f07928a92?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Brad DeLong notes</a><span>, educated professional types have had a long period of security, in which new innovations disrupted blue-collar work but not high-level white-collar work. That’s probably over now. But if educated progressive types don’t roll with the changes, and figure out how to use the new technology to their advantage, they could find themselves left behind by the tide of history — and the consequences will be worse than dirty butts and poorly cut pizza. </span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: Second, they have the capital and infrastructure to buy new pizza wheels instead of sharpening their old ones. promised to make America great again, he clearly wanted among other things to start throwing our military weight around. As </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0a33d10-04fc-4512-a92b-723f688bd08f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Timothy Snyder</a><span> says,</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The attack on Iran began with a </span><em>longing</em><span> -- a subjective sense that violence is pleasurable and can bring a utopia in which desires become reality. In the statements of President Trump and Defense Secretary Hegseth, such a utopia of violence is palpable.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Such a longing is always destructive even when, like Trump and Hegseth, one has inherited control of a powerful military. That military may not have been as powerful as many people imagined: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3735a3df-883e-4f3f-88ad-9dc62a7e3fca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Phillips O’Brien</a><span> argues that what he calls the “rot” in America’s armed forces began before Trump II. Still, America’s military was an impressive institution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And under Trump that institution is suffering rapid degradation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hegseth, reflecting attitudes widely held on the far right, came in asserting that wokeness had made the military weak, that the pursuit of diversity had led to the promotion of incompetent officers and that concern for liberal pieties had undermined the “warrior spirit” and focus on “lethality” that, he imagined, bring strength.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">With these people, however, every accusation is a confession. The Trumpists, it turns out, have prioritized their “anti-woke” ideology over military effectiveness. They have given free rein to bigotry, rejecting distinguished, highly regarded Black and female officers in favor of politically loyal white men. Cronyism has also played a destructive role, as I’ll explain shortly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Let’s look at the three axes of military degradation: Ideology, bigotry and corruption/cronyism.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Ideology</em><span>: Last week the New York Times </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cfcc87b4-38bb-4698-9fa2-3a6f5dbb0555?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reported</a><span> a major health crisis at an Air Force base:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A major flu outbreak has sickened nearly 160 troops at Lackland Air Force Base in Texas less than two months after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that U.S. troops would no longer be required to be vaccinated for the flu, defense officials said.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3ff80b21-1898-41d2-91c9-0e3b30c7ea74?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">wrote about</a><span> the end of the vaccination requirement when it was announced. It was obviously terrible policy: Vaccination shouldn’t be a matter of individual choice when spreading infections can impair military effectiveness. And you know who understood that? George Washington, who made smallpox inoculations mandatory in the Continental Army during the American Revolution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Vaccination, however, has become a front in the culture war. And Hegseth evidently considered being politically correct, MAGA style, more important than national security.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Bigotry:</em><span> Harry Truman desegregated the U.S. military in 1948. Over the years the military has come to be seen as a model for overcoming racial barriers, arguably one of our greatest national success stories in that regard. Three years ago the Pentagon commemorated the 75</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> anniversary of Truman’s decision. The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/13b22762-6bd9-4c0c-b451-2029a080c170?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">press release</a><span> was titled “U.S. military integration spawned peerless fighting force.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hegseth, however, judges officers not by the content of their character but by the color of their skin or their gender.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the Times has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/941048d1-6d3f-4c72-87a0-8a7d855b01ab?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reported</a><span>, Hegseth has fired or sidelined more than two dozen generals and admirals, disproportionately Black or female. As the Times reports, these high-profile actions are part of a larger story. Decisions about promotions within the military are normally made by serving officers:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">By law, one-star and two-star officers are chosen by promotion selection boards made up of senior military officers. The meetings are so confidential that board members are not permitted to tell others that they are part of the process.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Hegseth has been intervening in the promotion process. He has claimed that his new promotion system is focused on “warfighting ability,” but as the Times notes,</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In practice, though, his approach has made it harder for Black and female officers to get promoted to senior ranks, even when their records are exemplary.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Furthermore, promotions have been denied to officers who have spoken favorably about diversity or vaccines, even though those comments were made as part of then-current military policy.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">How much has this environment pushed competent officers out of the military? To what extent has it turned the officers that remain into yes-men — and I do mean men — unwilling to offer critical feedback on politically motivated decisions?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Cronyism</em><span>: On Monday the Pentagon’s artificial intelligence chief </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9d34cc91-a73e-4793-9015-e6d1bc6ec630?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">claimed</a><span> that Elon Musk’s Grok chatbot “enabled U.S. forces to deploy over 2,000 munitions to 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours during Operation Epic Fury.” Did that include the missile strikes that killed </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59a1611f-e6b4-44c4-8ad8-8b44d1cd5917?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">120 schoolchildren</a><span> on the first day of the war?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Pentagon made this statement as the Trump administration is trying to protect xAI, which runs Grok (and has now been folded into SpaceX) from a lawsuit alleging that its Memphis datacenter is illegally polluting the air.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So wait: </span><em>Grok</em><span> is running the war? By all accounts, Grok is greatly inferior to rival large language models operated by Anthropic and OpenAI. Indeed, federal agencies, when given a choice, have overwhelmingly rejected Grok. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4a5a58c7-6fc0-4267-9ed2-5fa050a59978?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Reuters</a><span> reports that of more than 400 reported government uses of AI that named a vendor, only 3 involved xAI or Grok.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not incidentally, Musk has made great efforts to train Grok not to give what he considers woke answers — efforts that led the model to spew </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73f96967-f365-47dc-aeaf-30f0107da79e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">racist and antisemitic content</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So why is the U.S. military using Grok — not just in some ordinary application, but to run a war? Officials claim that Grok has unique capabilities, but this surely looks like an attempt to promote the business of a Trump supporter and comrade in bigotry. And if Grok is inferior to available alternatives, which it probably is, this favoritism is directly endangering national security.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Not surprisingly, a war that both Trump and Hegseth declared would last a few short weeks has now turned into a military disaster with no clear end in sight other than a humiliating retreat. They ignored clear indicators that such a war was unwinnable because there was no plausible way to keep the Strait of Hormuz open, let alone force regime change in Iran. But even if we account for the epic idiocy of this war, U.S. forces have performed far worse than expected. Despite plenty of advance warning of the perils of drone warfare from the war in Ukraine, the U.S. military was caught flatfooted by the Iranian drone menace. As a result, it suffered massive destruction at our bases and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/39673c1e-a833-4416-a3b0-4d47c5b24ad9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">heavy aircraft losses</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The American military needs to have a reckoning with what has gone so badly wrong in the Iran war. But that won’t happen under the current commander-in-chief. Trump and Hegseth, who call themselves patriots, have subordinated national security to their personal prejudice, egoism and corruption. And from their point of view the loss of military professionalism, meritocracy and honor, along with the devastating loss of America’s reputation, is acceptable collateral damage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca0c642d-90ea-496d-ae2c-709b9da72fd9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/KCzORgC1NpM" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">When I was a kid, I loved to play the game SimCity (and its sequels SimCity 2000 and SimCity 3000), where you got to play urban planner. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What “urban planning” meant in this context was mainly that you planned </span><em>infrastructure</em><span> — the road and possibly rail networks needed to be laid out, electrical transmission needed rights-of-way, and you had to build stuff like parks and police stations and schools and fire stations. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, there was also zoning. </p><div worked basically like this: </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A city needs to have electricity to grow, which means it needs power plants. But power plants cause pollution and people don’t want to live in their shadow, so you can zone industrial land near your power plant, because industrial users won’t mind the pollution. But of course those industrial areas generate their own pollution! </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And you want to zone for residences far away from pollution or other undesirable land uses (like the garbage dumps introduced in SimCity 3000). You probably want to put your residential land near nice amenities such as water. You also want to make sure that things like parks and schools are located near residential zoning so people can use them. Commercial zones make a nice buffer between residential and industrial, but it’s also good to sprinkle some commerce around so you don’t end up with homes that are located a million miles away from anywhere to shop. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When I was in college, I got the chance to take a non-credit seminar about urban planning led by a former mayor. One of the conceits was that we were going to play SimCity 3000, and she was going to use it as a model to discuss planning issues. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One of the first things I learned was that real-world urban planning is much more complicated than it’s portrayed in the game. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But strikingly, it’s much more complicated </span><em>overwhelmingly in bad ways</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not that the game, with its emphasis on linear infrastructure and separating homes from pollution nuisances, is an oversimplification of urban life. It’s that real-world urban planning is a massive over-complication of what actually needs to be planned. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">You had one job</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Relative to totally chaotic city growth, I would say urban planning as a profession brought basically one good idea to the table. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That idea is that a coherent street grid, perhaps with a hierarchy of street widths distinguishing roads meant for local traffic from broader thoroughfares, is a better idea than roads just going willy-nilly. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A derivative of this idea is the notion that medieval-style cities with totally chaotic webs of streets can be improved by superimposing some long boulevards on the underlying chaos. That’s what Haussmann built for Paris, and Berlin also has some major boulevards such as Wilhelmstrasse and Unter den Linden. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This all makes it easier for people to get around cities; there are network benefits to having streets connect to each other in an orderly way.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Note, though, that this one idea is extremely old. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/056a0158-481b-47c5-9a27-b231302b15ff?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Roman Paris had a street grid</a><span>. This idea was un-invented in the Medieval West as part of a total collapse of state capacity. It eventually made a comeback, and you can see its influence in the New Town of Edinburgh and Eixample in Barcelona, plus of course most cities in North America. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But even this one good idea is honestly just not that important. Retrofitting chaotic street webs with a handful of big boulevards works fine. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Beyond that, London and Boston function essentially fine with their disorganized streets. There are some downsides, of course. It’s hard to construct robust bus routes in Boston because a bus usually works best if it can go straight on a big street and count on intersecting with other bus lines that go straight on other big streets. But it’s basically fine. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Similarly, while ideally you do want to set aside space for parks and other civic amenities </span><em>in advance</em><span> rather than shoehorning them into already built-up areas, it’s not the end of the world if you don’t. If a residential neighborhood springs up that has zero parks in it and that makes the neighborhood unpleasant, then land values will be relatively low, which makes it easier to retroactively obtain land and build parks. If land values are incredibly high such that it’s infeasible to build a park, then maybe people like the park-less neighborhood just fine and there’s no need to build one. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s not to advocate for a total lack of foresight; it’s just to emphasize that the risks here are asymmetrical. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you under-plan an area by not anticipating what its future civic needs will look like, you create some waste. But what overly prescriptive planning does in practice is create massive waste in all dimensions. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The denial of tradeoffs</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The crucial thing that’s missing from urban planning, day-in and day-out, is an appreciation of the virtues of markets. See this recent discussion between two commercial-real-estate professionals about cities deciding that they love mixed-use buildings with apartments above retail and that they are going to make ground 16px;"><span>The really infuriating thing about this, though, is that the same cities that try to make mixed-use development mandatory on certain parcels of land also make both mixed-use development and multifamily housing in general illegal on the </span><em>vast majority</em><span> of their land. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s not like they </span><em>actually</em><span> love traditional urbanism with apartments and ground floor retail and people walking to local commerce. They mostly ban that! </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But then when they decide to allow it, they form a picture in their head of their ideal urban village and try to make that mandatory. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Even then, though, their idea of how to create idealized neighborhoods is bizarre. Planners come up with all kinds of ideas about setbacks and “anti-massing” rules and the alleged evils of buildings casting shadows that have nothing to do with how any beloved world-famous neighborhood works. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now what’s true is that a lot of buildings in traditional neighborhoods have very real downsides. But the built environment is reacting to the fact that when space is valuable, it’s not a good idea to waste it on a random two-foot strip of grass. Someone will happily occupy a lower-floor apartment that doesn’t get much light in order to live in central Paris. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course a richer person will just pay more and get an apartment with better light. But the point is that unless you are infinitely wealthy, you can’t have everything that you might conceivably desire. In a successful neighborhood, the land itself is very expensive and valuable. That means people end up compromising on certain things. The apartment I grew up in was mostly fantastic, but it was annoyingly loud at night, which is the price you pay for living on a bustling street. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, I live on a quiet street that is </span><em>near</em><span> a bustling street. That’s better! But also, D.C. land is generally a lot cheaper than New York land, so it’s easier to afford to be picky. And of course there are people who do live right on the bustling street and deal with the noise. It’s not ideal, but conditional on the bustling street existing, it’s better for some people to live there than to make it illegal for people to expose themselves to street noise. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reality is that real estate involves a ton of complicated tradeoffs, which is </span><em>the</em><span> thing that markets are good for. But instead, we get planning that has a kind of paranoid terror of anywhere ever getting overcrowded or messy when in reality it’s fine if it sometimes is.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The city as engine</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In retrospect, a subtle piece of the secret sauce in SimCity is that not only do you have to deal with normal revenue/spending budget issues, but the simple fact of zoning a plot of land costs money. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This doesn’t really make sense. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the real world, building infrastructure costs money. But drawing lines on a map is so cheap that it might as well be free. For that matter, while </span><em>actually constructing</em><span> roads and schools and parks and libraries and police stations costs money, simply designating space for them on a map is basically free. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But in SimCity, the map </span><em>is</em><span> the territory. You just build roads by drawing them on a map; you don’t plan the roads on a map and then go build them somewhere. And you can’t even do the zoning until you save up the money. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As a result, your “planning” of the city is really building an economic engine. You start with the power plant and some industrial zoning and a road connecting that job hub to some residences. That little seed gives you the tax revenue necessary to start building out the rest of the map. And the whole game is built around what’s essentially a model economy. The amount of residential demand is in part a function of the available jobs. And the amount of demand for retail is in part a function of the size of the residential population. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When you’re doing it right, you have a flywheel where jobs attract residents, residents attract service jobs, and those service jobs attract more residents. The game does not officially have a goal or “victory” conditions, but implicit in the basic design is that you are </span><em>trying</em><span> to build a large and economically successful city with low crime and good schools where growth fuels demand. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In real life, the typical planning paradigm treats the city like an art project.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Wouldn’t it be nice if this set of mid-rise buildings was accompanied by ground floor retail?” I’m sure it would be nice! And it would be even nicer with some more trees. And of course the units in the building should be spacious and there should be ample off-street parking, and it all looks great in a rendering. But does it actually work? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the rendering, the weather is always pleasant and plenty of people are always milling around. And the street is always depicted as pleasantly busy, never overly crowded. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Think this through, though. The weather isn’t always nice. It’s not always Saturday afternoon. The neighborhood needs to exist 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days of the year, through all four seasons. If it’s not overcrowded under optimal conditions, it’s going to be massively </span><em>undercrowded</em><span> across huge swaths of time. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A restaurant where it’s easy to get a table at 8 p.m. on a Friday is going to go out of business. By the same token, Midtown Manhattan at lunchtime on a Wednesday is a pretty annoying place to be — not because of some tragic planning flaw but because that’s what a thriving hub of commerce is like at a peak time. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We’re not going to impose congestion pricing on the sidewalk, so it </span><em>has</em><span> to get overcrowded at times or else you’ve overbuilt. It’s true that this is not as aesthetically pleasing as a place permanently frozen into a kind of medium-chill level of usage. But that’s not how actual spaces or businesses work. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And all the efforts to create a little more green space, a little more light, a little more parking, a little more this and a little more that end up imposing massive hidden costs relative to the messiness of market-driven outcomes.  </p><p And that includes the imposition of de facto tolls, whatever they are called.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is no mystery about Trump’s surrender: He’s desperate to end the war because he is paying a steep political price for high gasoline prices, and the midterms are only 4 ½ months away.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But can Trump rehabilitate his standing with American voters by throwing in the towel? Probably not, for both economic and political reasons. I would argue that there are four points of slippage between Trump’s political goals and what is likely to happen.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>The state of the Strait</em><span>: Even if the war is truly over, it will take time to return world oil supplies to normal levels. First, there has been substantial damage to the Persian Gulf’s infrastructure, which will take months, if not years, to repair. Second, many oil tankers are now in the wrong place and it will take weeks or months to move them. Third, some shipping channels are at risk from stray mines. Lastly, the world met the Hormuz crisis in part by running down oil inventories, which will now need to be rebuilt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true that a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/29a50c53-f9f9-49a2-acb0-94dbcf4b4ea9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">surge</a><span> in </span><em>Iranian</em><span> oil exports has begun thanks to the lifting of the U.S. blockade. This will add to global oil supplies but will also strengthen the regime. But despite this surge of Iranian shipments, prices of oil futures — promises to buy or sell oil on specified dates — indicate that the oil markets expect oil prices to decline at only a slow rate for which would point to gasoline prices $0.25-$0.37 higher per gallon. Yet gasoline is currently almost $1 a gallon higher than it was before the war.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So if the “rockets and feathers” pattern continues to apply, gasoline prices will be elevated for months to come, thwarting Trumpist hopes of quick political relief from capitulating to Iran.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Prices beyond gasoline</em><span>: As you can see in the chart above, the war on Iran sent the price of diesel fuel soaring by significantly more than the price of gasoline. Unlike gasoline, which is mainly purchased by consumers, diesel is mainly used by businesses, for trucking and industrial uses. So the surge in diesel prices led to a surge in business costs rather than a direct burden on consumers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">True, businesses do eventually pass higher costs on to consumers. The key word, however, is “eventually.” This means that there is probably substantial Iran war-induced inflation still in the pipeline.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Nor were soaring prices of diesel the only cost the war imposed on businesses. The Persian Gulf is normally a key supplier of many chemicals, whose prices soared when the Strait of Hormuz was closed. For example, the price of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e2ffa4e2-dabb-4013-bfc6-5ac6d03b35fe?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">urea</a><span>, a key fertilizer with industrial uses as well, temporarily rose by 75 percent when the Strait was closed. Again, some of the effect of these cost shocks still hasn’t hit consumer prices.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Moreover, the economy is delivering inflationary shocks independent of the war. Notably, the AI/datacenter boom has driven a rapid rise in electricity prices and huge increases in the prices of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a0921297-1a31-4c69-852d-cd45ab5fc78e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">memory chips</a><span>, which are used in almost all consumer electronics, from smartphones to laptops to game consoles. The AI boom has also pushed up interest rates on mortgages and consumer loans. Oh, and Trump’s cuts to Obamacare subsidies are causing many Americans’ health insurance costs to soar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So while consumers are getting some relief at the gas pump, they’re facing persistent sticker shock on many other goods. It’s safe to predict that consumers won’t be in a celebratory mood on D-I [defeat by Iran] Day. Instead, they are likely to feel that any claims of victory are Pyrrhic at best.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>The cost of broken promises</em><span>: We have just endured the second big gasoline price shock of the past five years. In fact, that’s what I </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5cb97825-392c-45d8-bf60-55a19015a371?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">have argued</a><span>, and a majority of Americans now say that the economy was better under Biden than under Trump. However, that argument is beside the point for analyzing the effect of the Trump surrender. The point, instead, is that once a leader has lost the public’s economic trust, that trust doesn’t come back just because gasoline prices have receded.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I would add that it may be especially hard for the Trumpists to make the case that things have turned around when they were never willing to admit that anything was wrong in the first place, insisting even as prices soared that we were living in a “golden age.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So will Trump’s surrender to Iran rescue him and his party from a blue wave in November? York Governor George Pataki at a press conference in 2002. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad9b1d8c-ca87-46db-aed0-018281f5b816?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Brooks Kraft</a><span> via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Twenty-five years ago, I was a summer intern in the office of New York Senator Chuck Schumer. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">He was a sort of unusual case at the time. At the age of 50, he was relatively young for a senator and in his first term, having been elected to the seat in 1998. But he was first elected to the New York State Assembly when he was fresh out of law school at 23 years old and jumped to the U.S. House of Representatives when he was 29. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So he managed to be both a young senator and also a veteran politician. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s also hard to imagine given contemporary politics, but his 1998 victory over incumbent Republican Senator Al D’Amato was considered something of an underdog victory at the time. Politics was simply much less polarized. New York City had a moderate Republican mayor and the state had a moderate Republican governor, so there was no particular reason to think that a moderate Republican senator from Long Island couldn’t keep winning re-election indefinitely. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It was just a different time, politically, when basically every statewide office was considered at least potentially contestable if you could raise money, and the House battleground was much wider. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of the point here is just that I’m old. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My responsibilities as an intern included tasks like cutting articles out of print newspapers in order to fax a daily packet of clippings to the senator’s different offices around the state. I would also grab press releases hot off the printer and fax</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> them to various media outlets. Photocopiers and fax machines were also a big part of my job during my internship at Rolling Stone the previous summer. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Literally nobody would perform such tasks these days. But it occurs to me that this is a situation where age brings some wisdom. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Precisely because politics was so different back then, a much larger share of working politicians thought a lot about persuasion and about swing voters. Political staffing is a young person’s game, and for a while now the whole concept of trying to persuade swing voters and beat Republicans has been a niche pursuit that only a tiny minority of elected Democrats focus on. As a result, staffers don’t really receive even “summer internship brown bag lunch” levels of training in how it’s done. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Obviously a lot of what Schumer and my direct boss had to say about this is now as outdated as the list of speed dial</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> codes taped up to the wall by the fax machine. A lot of it, though, remains extremely relevant today. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The voters who matter don’t follow politics</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Media consumption habits have changed enormously in the past 25 years. One constant, though, and something Schumer’s communications director really drummed into me, is this: </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The media consumption habits of persuadable voters are </span><em>very</em><span> different from the habits of political junkies. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is important to drill yourself on because the people who work in politics professionally are political junkies. Back in 2001, that meant staffers paying attention to publications like Roll Call and Congressional Quarterly and watching programs like CNN’s “Inside Politics” on weekday afternoons or the Sunday-morning interview shows. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Plenty of non-professionals watched those shows, too. But the point was that the kind of people sufficiently interested in politics to want to watch Tim Russert or Judy Woodruff interview politicians are very hard to persuade. People who care a lot about politics tend to have firm partisan convictions. Even if they’re cross-pressured or willing to be occasional crossover voters, the cross-pressures are probably deeply rooted. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As a politician, the people you really want to target with your casual messaging are people whose views about politics are pretty fuzzy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The fuzziest people in the country back in 2001 were probably tuning in to local television news to get sports scores, weather forecasts, and service-y news. Nobody who works in politics professionally cares much what’s on WIVT in Binghamton. And the audience for WIVT in Binghamton probably doesn’t care that much about politics. But as a result, the highest-impact thing the senator’s staff could do was get him on WIVT in Binghamton saying or doing something popular. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of our real messaging coups that summer was when we got Yankees manager Joe Torre and some local hospital executives to do an event with Schumer promoting blood donations, but also trying to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0dc7c54b-1bf9-4394-ab67-59e553c80b44?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">help New York-area hospitals out with a serious policy problem</a><span> that was playing out in D.C. at the time. The Joe Torre angle, probably more than the substance of it, attracted a lot of attention from local television stations. So we got the senator in front of an audience that doesn’t necessarily care about politics and had him talking about something that doesn’t play as partisan or “political” in a classic sense. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">People like small wins</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At that particular point in human history, Verizon — which at the time was the local telephone provider in the northeastern United States — was heavily promoting two special features. One was *66 (the “busy signal fix”), which you could dial if you were calling a friend and got a busy signal.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">³</span><span> The other was *69 (“not in time, press star six nine”), which was essentially a redial function. The idea that led to *69 was that someone might call you, but then hang up before you were able to make it to your phone and pick up. By hitting *69, you could call back whoever had called you.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The trick was, you’d get charged if you used those features. I believe the fees were disclosed in the fine print of the ads promoting the services, but they were not disclosed in real time when you used them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some friend of Schumer’s got hit with a whopper of a bill based on one of his kids going nuts with the *66, and he did something relatively insubstantial about it, like write a letter to the Federal Communications Commission asking them to promulgate regulations banning this. But it made for a big press conference. I helped stage one in New York City, and it got so much attention that the senator wound up taking it on the road and promoting the same initiative in several upstate cities. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now, in retrospect, I would say that this was not really one of the most significant public policy issues in George W. Bush’s America. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: ltr;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="pencraft pc-reset button-wrapper" style="text-decoration: unset;list-style: none;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button subscribe-btn outline" href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuc2xvd2JvcmluZy5jb20vYWNjb3VudCIsInAiOjE5OTg1NTc2MCwicyI6MTU5MTg1LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6Mjk3MTk2MDMwLCJpYXQiOjE3ODIyMDk0MjAsImV4cCI6MjA5Nzc4NTQyMCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.AIBzfz18DE6FusyU-61gp2LiMafnkT5TRPolBol3DmA?" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;background-color: transparent;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;text-decoration: none !important;border: 1px solid #04b2a5;margin: 0 auto;background: transparent;color: #04b2a5;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><img class="check-icon static" src="https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Fvey!,w_40,c_scale,f_png,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack.com%2Ficon%2FLucideCheck%3Fv%3D4%26height%3D40%26fill%3Dtransparent%26stroke%3D%252304B2A5%26strokeWidth%3D3.6" width="20" height="20" style="border: none;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;display: inline-block;margin: -2px 8px 0 0;max-width: 20px" alt=""><span style="text-decoration: none;">Subscribed</span></a></div></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t even remember whether the F.C.C. did what we wanted. By the time this came around, the features in question were already somewhat obsolete since more and more people had call waiting and caller ID. Cell phones were, obviously, also exploding in popularity at this time and generally had those as standard features. So this whole thing really did not matter. Even at the time, it was clearly pretty trivial relative to the huge stakes around the Bush tax cuts, Medicare coverage of prescription drugs, abortion rights, and whatever else the Senate was working on at the time. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The problem-solving ethos</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Critically, though, Schumer was okay with the wins being small. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In contemporary politics, the torch of calling out small scams and vowing to protect consumers has been carried forward by people like Elizabeth Warren, Rohit Chopra, and Lina Khan. Indeed, I think when she first arrived on the scene, Warren struck Schumer as a kindred spirit. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The difference, though, is that the modern-day anti-scam warriors wear their ideologies on their sleeve. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Schumer approach to the “junk fee” issue would have been to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/63ec0c14-f594-4343-8641-670e9edce602?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">ban hotels from charging non-optional destination fees</a><span> and then say nice things about everyone when they stopped doing it. Maybe talk about how great and convenient online travel booking is compared to how things used to be, and that’s why it’s important to crack down on abusive ways of characterizing your prices. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The point is that swing voters don’t really like politics or care much about it, and they definitely aren’t interested in big-picture ideological clashes. You want to at least portray yourself as someone who woke up in the morning, heard about a problem, thought about it all day, and is now here with a solution. The people in the Warren tradition aren’t like that at all. To them, everything is a totalizing clash between their ideological vision and an implacable opposition driven by corruption. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a result, instead of having the spirit of a “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c8499555-00e2-4b8a-bb42-f0aa931f6eea?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">7 on Your Side</a><span>” local television news segment, Biden-era regulators got a reputation as anti-business crusaders who made more enemies than friends. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In his 2007 book, “Positively American,” Schumer wrote about efforts to broker a bipartisan deal that would have opened more land in Alaska for oil drilling but also increased fuel efficiency standards on American cars. He laments that it didn’t come together because of interest group opposition on both sides. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This taps into </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d7b52dfb-f188-4bd4-ae2c-2f6525cf37e3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">how most Americans conceptualize corruption</a><span> — they believe there’s a “problem-solving” mode that politicians could tap into if they wanted and make all the country’s troubles go away. They see the persistence of political conflict as a problem per se. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I of course get why Trump-era Democrats fetishize “fighters,” but I think it’s really important to understand that the purpose of fighting is to win, and you don’t win contested voters over by seeming stubborn. You </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/521794bd-4efd-410b-bdfd-9ca53483fd91?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">don’t need to call it moderation</a><span>, but there is a real difference between the problem-solving mode and the ideological-warrior mode. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">We used to have politicians in this country</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Everyone more or less knows that there are fewer swing seats and crossover voters than there used to be, and less ticket-splitting. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I think people still underrate how much this has influenced the U.S. political system. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It used to be that even if there were plenty of safe House seats, any kind of statewide office was at least in principle contestable. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In 1998, when Schumer was making his first Senate run, New York had a Republican governor, New York City had a Republican mayor, and he was taking on a Republican incumbent. It was a solidly blue state in presidential politics at the time, but you just assumed that every statewide office would be visibly contested. As a result, basically every ambitious politician spent at least some time thinking about swing voters and persuasion — even if it wasn’t important for winning re-election, it was important for upward mobility. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Today’s politics isn’t like that.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Michigan, specifically, a Democratic Party primary voter might say, “I like Abdul’s message, but I think Haley is the one who can win the seat.” But there aren’t a lot of states like that. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are politicians like Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris who’ve had very successful careers in Democratic Party politics without ever having beaten a Republican in a contested race. And increasingly there are people like Maria Cantwell and Schumer himself who did it once, back in the day, but will never have to again. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For most elected officials — and therefore most staffers and most campaign operatives — coalition-management is the only thing that actually matters, and it’s quite alien to imagine an incumbent sitting around worrying about persuasion. In retrospect, Schumer didn’t really need to be sweating all this small stuff in the summer of 2001. He never faced a serious opponent again. But at the time, it was reflexive — most people working in politics were persuasion-oriented and it was kind of in the water. Over the past 10 or 15 years, though, that’s become a niche pursuit, and there’s this huge cohort of members and operatives who never think about it. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up before Xi Jinping came to power, Chinese state television ran a 12-part miniseries called </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/12e34db2-cce3-4301-993c-3fd78286d6dd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The Rise of the Great Powers</a></em><span>. It was based on Paul Kennedy’s book, </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4ad0cf2d-b6fe-4901-a187-71532bf360cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers</a></em><span>, first published in 1989, and included interviews with the author, but also expanded on the source material. The show went through a bunch of historical examples of great powers — the Netherlands, Great Britain, France, Germany, Japan, Russia/USSR, and the U.S. — and tried to explain each one’s rise (and, if applicable, its fall). The implication was, of course, that China ought to become the next great power in the sequence.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I haven’t seen the series, but I’ve read Kennedy’s book, and its ideas are powerful and provocative. The most interesting idea is that countries become great powers due to their mastery of the most important technologies of the day — gunpowder, sailing ships, steam power, mass production, steel, the combustion engine, industrial chemicals, electricity, airplanes, and so on.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> The U.S., he argued, mastered the key technologies of the 20th century better than any other nation. To his list, we should add semiconductors, computers, and the internet. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are some interesting unexplored corollaries of Kennedy’s idea. Although he attributes great-power decline to hubris and overstretch, it’s also possible to imagine that leading nations fall behind due to </span><em>technological disruption</em><span>. Britain’s industrial revolution made mercantile trade less pivotal as a source of national wealth, so the Netherlands fell behind. Britain failed to seize dominance of aviation and combustion engines the way the U.S., Germany, and (to a lesser degree) Russia did, so its early advantage in steam power became less important. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Today, everyone recognizes that artificial intelligence is the most important technology in the world — not just because of what it can do directly, but because of its potential to accelerate </span><em>other</em><span> technologies. Right now, the United States is leading in that industry, thanks to its pioneering role in AI research, but also to its mastery of semiconductors (along with its network of allies) and its skillful and timely use of export controls. Chinese AI models are officially nipping at the heels of Anthropic and OpenAI, but actually the gap is bigger than advertised. Here’s </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/151c7aef-f68d-4168-b220-5d6ed5fe56f7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">The Economist</a></em><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In reality, America’s lead is probably bigger than four months. Open-source models, many of them Chinese, tend to score better on public benchmarks than private ones, says Havard Tveit Ihle of the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment…[O]n private tests, America’s lead nearly doubled, to eight to ten months[.]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And here’s a chart from NIST, In earlier days, this was just a matter of pushing lots of current through wires. Today, it includes three other key technologies: </span><strong>modern batteries</strong><span>, </span><strong>permanent-magnet electric motors</strong><span>, and </span><strong>power electronics</strong><span>. These three critical inventions all came about at the turn of the century. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Modern batteries — mostly lithium-ion batteries, but also including some things like sodium-ion batteries — allow you to move energy around in far smaller packages than combustion engines can, because you don’t need to have all that engine machinery. AI represents the culmination of a century of progress in information technology — “bits”, as they say — that had coincided with a long stagnation in physical technology (“atoms”). Electric tech breaks the stagnation in “atoms”, returning us to a regime in which our ability to manipulate the physical world keeps getting better and better.
