Its whole government has bent its fearsome power toward making sure that China, not America, controls the physical technologies that will dominate the 21st century. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s succeeding, thanks in part to America’s own blinkered complacency and reluctance to adopt new innovations. So far, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d14452af-8b1c-46e8-976a-32ed1f9689f7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">only Tesla has managed</a><span> to keep America in the electric race, and its chances of singlehandedly matching China in the long term are basically nil. The rest of America is utterly sleeping on the electric revolution. Political conservatives have chosen to believe that technologies like electric cars are hippie-dippy bullshit, despite Elon’s exhortations. Big old-line companies like Ford and GM are caught in the innovator’s dilemma, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a90dd90f-0f13-41cd-8776-e801fb9a5552?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">institutionally incapable</a><span> of embracing disruptive change. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finally, a few Americans are waking up to the fact that physical technologies are important, that something big has changed since the 1970s, and that America will need more than fancy AI to stay competitive in the 21st century. Here are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f352ec3e-a1a9-4603-b3ac-2a10056179a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Simon Johnson and Elisabeth B. Reynolds</a><span> in Bloomberg:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Washington has woken up to the importance of AI — and especially to the “AI race” against China…[But] artificial intelligence is…hardly the only technology that matters…In the case of drones, the new critical force in modern warfare, we find a familiar pattern to US industrial development: Invent it here, make it there.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Johnson and Reynolds stop short of full recognition of the unity and importance of electric technology, but they’re on the right track. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a5bcaaad-db4a-41a4-8a91-03b4dc43f867?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">A recent article</a><span> in the New York Times focused on the importance of electric technologies in the U.S.-China competition. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Republicans in the U.S. government are also — </span><em>very</em><span> belatedly — realizing that the electric revolution is real. They’re funding a whole slew of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/27cb568c-0645-47a4-beeb-3b6c3ff5451e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">drone startups</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bab70160-858a-4244-9856-20da7a24a278?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">rare earth companies</a><span>, and other companies that promise to break America’s dependence on China for electric supply chains. Without that demand, companies that make batteries, motors, and power electronics will find it a lot harder to scale up. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meanwhile, absolutely no one seems to be doing anything about the U.S.’ electric infrastructure deficit. Even as China races toward becoming the world’s “first electrostate”, the Trump administration is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ace921cc-2805-412d-a2a6-71152ea3bd50?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">attacking solar power</a><span> (with some success), even as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4cb27636-13ee-4457-9ceb-14de45fe0052?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">local NIMBYs block</a><span> solar projects and transmission lines all over the country. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To me, this all speaks to a continued lack of understanding of the electric revolution. Americans perceive this momentous event only dimly through the fog — unlike the Chinese, they do not understand what the key electric technologies are, when they were invented, why they’re important, and how they work together. And because there is no understanding of the electric revolution, there is no concerted policy push to do all of the many, many things it would take — from permitting reform to industrial subsidies to R&D programs — to give the United States a fighting chance to master this technological revolution. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">AI is an incredibly powerful technology, but it’s a mistake to simply assume that whoever masters it will also be the master of the physical world. The messy world of atoms still matters, and if America can’t finance, permit, or compete in the world of electric technology, a billion “geniuses in a data center” won’t necessarily give us mastery of drones, robots, electric vehicles, and so on. Some Paul Kennedy of the future, writing an epitaph for America’s epic run as a great power, may conclude that our failure to master electric technology was a factor in our relative decline.</p><div
